newsitem.title: FRANCE: French budget good on EMU, soft in the centre.
newsitem.headline: French budget good on EMU, soft in the centre.

text.p: France's 1997 budget produces just what is called for by the EU's Maastricht treaty mathematics on monetary union but looks soft-centred against German efforts to purge state finances, economists said on Wednesday.
"It's really a compromise between the Maastricht rules and what their (parliamentary) majority and public opinion is pressing them for," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.
"This is not the tight budget once expected," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.
But a government target of reducing the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product was credible, he said.
"In a nutshell the 1997 budget implies that the French franc is most likely to be replaced by the euro in 1999 as scheduled."

Chaney added: "A quality gap might appear between Germany, where federal expenditures are supposed to be cut in absolute terms, and France where the political compromise has finally resulted in a relatively soft budget."

The French budget coupled tax cuts of 25 billion francs ($4.85 billion) next year with savings of 60 billion francs on central government spending for 1997 to keep it at the same level as last year once inflation and mechanical increments are taken into account.
It foresees a central government budget deficit of 283.7 billion francs versus a forecast 288 billion this year, which was seen as a smaller reduction than many had been expecting.
"They could have tightened more and targeted something like 2.8 percent (of GDP)," Brossard at ABN Amro in Paris said.
One of the reasons for the bigger-than-expected central government budget deficit was pessimistic assumptions on the forecast rise in net tax receipts, he said.
Tax revenues are expected to rise by just 1.14 percent next year after the tax reform is taken into account.

Transfer of funds from France Telecom and state bank CDC, respectively 37.5 billion and 18 billion francs, plus 12 billion from welfare debt repayment fund CADES, will bring total deficit to the Maastricht target of three percent of GDP.
Smith Barney economist Paul Horne said the budget was "on the path of the spirit of monetary union" but he was worried that the government was taking a soft route.

"It is moving toward the three percent (deficit) of GDP for 1997. But the quality of the deficit reduction compares badly with Germany where we have been seeing some attacks on the structural problems," he told Reuters Financial Television.

Patrick Mange of Deutsche Bank said the government's move to stabilise spending would help credibility but more needed to be done to attack the structural side of the deficit. "The quality of the deficit reduction is very important," he said.
Economists said they did not believe that the budget would trigger the same kind of industrial unrest seen in late 1995.

"There is the possibility of social conflict but the difference with the social conflict at the end of 1995 is that we do not have a focal point to unify (people)," Mange said. "I see conflicts but not as messy as we saw in 1995."
Markets hardly reacted to the budget, largely because much of the details had been leaked in advance but also because it proved the commitment to meet the Maastricht deficit target.
"As long as the markets perceive the road to EMU remains intact, there's little reason for an attack on the franc or bonds," Jean-Francois Mercier, economist at Salomon Brothers, said.
Mange added what was important to markets now was whether economic growth would pick up.
"If growth decelerates instead of accelerates in the coming months, then markets would again doubt EMU which would destabilise the French franc." ($1=5.151 French Franc)
